disposition.note:
You were seen today for a follow-up visit regarding your recent pneumonia. You are still experiencing a cough, runny nose, and post-nasal drip. You are also having back spasms related to your persistent cough. The good news is that your chest X-ray shows improvement compared to your last visit. Because you are still recovering, we are extending your antibiotic and adding medications to help manage your remaining symptoms.

Your Medications
Augmentin (amoxicillin/clavulanate) — Continue for 3 more days to complete your pneumonia treatment. Take as previously prescribed with food to reduce stomach upset.
Ipratropium bromide nasal spray (0.06%) — Spray 2 sprays in each nostril 3–4 times daily. This will help dry up your runny nose. Avoid spraying into your eyes. You will need to prime the pump with 7 sprays before first use.
Flonase (fluticasone) nasal spray — Spray 1–2 sprays in each nostril once daily. This helps reduce nasal inflammation, congestion, and post-nasal drip. Use daily for best results; it may take a few days to feel the full effect.
Tessalon Perles (benzonatate) 100 mg — Take 1 capsule by mouth 3 times daily as needed for cough. Swallow the capsule whole — do not chew, crush, or dissolve it, as this can cause numbness of the mouth and throat.
Methocarbamol (Robaxin) 750 mg — Take 1 tablet by mouth 3 times daily as needed for back spasms. This medication may cause drowsiness or dizziness. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how it affects you.

What to Expect
It is normal for a cough to linger for several weeks after pneumonia, even as the infection clears. Your X-ray is improving, which is a reassuring sign.
Prolonged coughing can strain the muscles in your back, causing spasms and soreness. The muscle relaxant should help ease this discomfort. As your cough improves, the back spasms should also resolve.
The nasal sprays and cough medication should help you feel more comfortable while your body continues to heal.
Continue to rest, stay well hydrated, and avoid smoking or secondhand smoke exposure.

When to Seek Medical Attention
Contact our office or seek medical care if you experience any of the following:
Fever (temperature above 100.4°F / 38°C)
Worsening shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Chest pain
Coughing up blood
Symptoms that worsen rather than improve after completing the antibiotic
Severe back pain, weakness, or numbness in your legs
Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that prevents you from taking your medications

Follow-Up
If your cough and symptoms have not improved within 2–3 weeks, please call our office to schedule a follow-up appointment for further evaluation. 
Please follow up with your Primary Care Physician and let them know about your recent illness.
